issues.legal_issue: A decision in an earlier suit for dissolution and accounts does not bar a later suit concerning entitlement to compensation for an acquired undertaking when the later entitlement was not decided in the earlier suit.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought dissolution of the partnership and an accounting while the licence and undertaking were still in existence.
The later suit sought a declaration that the licensee alone was entitled to compensation after the licence was revoked and the undertaking was taken over by the government.
Although the suits had some issues in common, the earlier suit did not determine whether the other contributors could recover their respective shares from the compensation.
issues.conclusion: The appeals concerning the later compensation suit were not barred by res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the general doctrine of res judicata prevent re-litigation of a matter finally decided between the parties; the relevant test is whether the issue was in substance tried and decided before. The Court discussed Lakshmi v. Bhuli and Narhari v. Sankar, and distinguished Sheodan Singh v. Mst. Daryao Kaur. It did not decide the broader question whether dismissal of one of multiple appeals from a common judgment necessarily bars another appeal, because the subject matter of the two suits differed.

predicates.appeal_from_later_compensation_suit: A party appeals in a suit concerning who is entitled to compensation for an acquired undertaking.
predicates.earlier_suit_sought_dissolution_and_acco: An earlier suit between relevant parties sought dissolution of a business arrangement and an accounting.
predicates.later_suit_sought_exclusive_compensation: The later suit sought a determination that one person alone was entitled to compensation for the undertaking.
predicates.compensation_entitlement_not_decided_ear: The earlier suit did not decide whether other contributors could claim shares of the compensation.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns compensation entitlement and the earlier dissolution-and-accounting suit did not decide that entitlement, the later compensation appeal is not barred by res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: People who contributed capital to acquire an undertaking may claim their proportionate shares of compensation replacing the undertaking even if the arrangement under which they contributed is void or becomes void.
material_facts: Several participants contributed money in accordance with their agreed shares towards the purchase of the undertaking and later contributed further capital.
The licensee was named as the sole licensee, but partnership deeds recorded the participants and their respective shares.
The government revoked the licence and took over the undertaking, and compensation for the undertaking was deposited in court.
The licensee claimed that he alone had funded the purchase and was entitled to the entire compensation, but the evidence established contributions by the other participants.
The later partnership deed recorded the shares according to which the compensation was to be distributed, after payment of outstanding liabilities.
issues.conclusion: The licensee was not entitled to the whole compensation; the participants named in the later partnership deed, or their successors, were entitled to share the net compensation in proportion to their recorded shares.
issues.legal_principle: Section 65 of the Indian Contract Act requires a person who received an advantage under an agreement discovered to be void, or under a contract that becomes void, to restore it or compensate the person from whom it was received. The Court relied on Budhu Lal v. Deccan Banking Company Ltd. in explaining that the section can apply even where an agreement was void from the outset but its invalidity was discovered later. Section 14 of the Partnership Act was also relevant to the treatment of property acquired with partnership capital as partnership assets. The Court held that the capital arrangement did not fall within sections 9(2) and 9(3) of the Indian Electricity Act merely because the licence stood in one participant’s name, but left undecided whether carrying on the electricity business in those circumstances was invalid. The right to recover contributed money did not depend on the validity of the partnership.

rule.if: appeal_from_sole_compensation_entitlement_decision and multiple_participants_contributed_acquisition_capital and undertaking_replaced_by_compensation and participant_shares_recorded and compensation_received_for_shared_asset

predicates.appeal_from_sole_compensation_entitlemen: A party appeals a decision that one person alone is entitled to compensation for an undertaking.
predicates.multiple_participants_contributed_acquis: More than one participant supplied money towards acquiring the undertaking.
predicates.undertaking_replaced_by_compensation: The undertaking was taken over or otherwise converted into a right to compensation.
predicates.participant_shares_recorded: A document records the participants’ respective shares in the arrangement.
predicates.compensation_received_for_shared_asset: A person received or controlled compensation for an asset acquired using the participants’ contributions.

issues.definition: Where an appeal concerns sole entitlement to compensation, multiple participants funded the undertaking, their shares were recorded, and compensation replaced the undertaking, the contributors are entitled to the net compensation in proportion to those shares.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to recover contributions is not time-barred when the participants were not aware that their arrangement was invalid until the invalidity was later disclosed and the claims were brought before or within the applicable limitation period after that discovery.
material_facts: The participants openly conducted the business and submitted accounts and balance sheets reflecting the partnership to the participants and the government.
The evidence did not establish that the participants knew their arrangement was illegal when they entered into it.
The government later notified the licensee that the partnership was illegal and subsequently revoked the licence.
The relevant suits were filed before or within the applicable period following the discovery of the alleged illegality.
issues.conclusion: The claims were not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court rejected the High Court’s view that the claims were barred under Article 62 of the Limitation Act. It relied on the circumstances showing that the participants were not aware of the alleged illegality before it was disclosed and held that the suits were not time-barred. This conclusion accompanied the Court’s application of section 65 of the Indian Contract Act to restoration of benefits under an agreement discovered to be void.

predicates.appeal_from_limitation_ruling_on_contrib: A party appeals a ruling on limitation in a claim to recover contributions made under a business arrangement.
predicates.participants_unaware_of_invalidity: The participants did not know that the arrangement was invalid when they made their contributions.
predicates.invalidity_disclosed_later: The arrangement’s alleged invalidity was disclosed to the participants only after they had made their contributions.
predicates.recovery_suit_filed_before_or_within_app: The recovery suit was filed before discovery of the invalidity or within the applicable limitation period after discovery.

issues.definition: If participants were unaware of an arrangement’s invalidity until it was later disclosed and they brought their recovery suit before or within the applicable period after discovery, their contribution-recovery claim is not time-barred.
